description: Hi! We're ChronoFlare! Different satellites do not observe fire in the same way. ChronoFlare helps researchers and environmental analysts explore historical fire activity while keeping sensor provenance, uncertainty and missing data visible.
summary:
ChronoFlare is a web application that helps researchers and environmental analysts explore historical fire activity while accounting for differences between MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

Using NASA FIRMS data and the official IBGE Pantanal boundary, we developed an interactive burning-activity calendar, year-to-year comparisons, a detection map, and a transparent scientific-evidence dashboard. Users can inspect native satellite records and calibrated estimates, including uncertainty intervals, missing observations, and each date’s role in model development or evaluation.

ChronoFlare addresses the challenge by harmonizing MODIS observations onto a VIIRS reference scale. Our frozen model passed a registered independent test covering 506 paired days across 40 eligible weeks, reducing weekly mean absolute error by approximately 35% against the matched uncalibrated benchmark.

The Pantanal is our validated pilot region. Publication requires complete Terra and Aqua inputs, resulting in limited availability in 2025–2026; no independent backward validation is claimed.

ChronoFlare makes historical comparisons more interpretable without hiding uncertainty or treating missing records as zero activity. It provides a foundation for broader regional validation and future seasonal analysis.
details:
We built ChronoFlare around a simple question: how can we compare fire activity over time when the satellites observing it do not see the same things?

NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS instruments have different resolutions and overpass times. Joining their records directly can make a change in observation look like a change in fire activity. We wanted to help people explore that history while understanding where the data support a comparison—and where they do not.

ChronoFlare is a web application built around the Brazilian Pantanal as a pilot region. It combines NASA FIRMS observations with the official IBGE biome boundary. Users can explore a burning-activity calendar, compare years, inspect satellite detections on a map, and examine the evidence behind our harmonization method.

The calendar keeps the original Terra, Aqua, and Suomi-NPP observations available separately. It also offers a calibrated series that estimates fire radiative power on a common VIIRS reference scale. Selecting a day reveals the estimate, its uncertainty interval, the observed S-NPP reference where available, and the uncalibrated MODIS benchmark. Missing observations stay missing.

Getting that calibration right was one of our biggest challenges. Our first candidate failed its validation checks. We kept that result, investigated what went wrong, and developed a second version. We then froze the revised model and evaluated it on previously unexamined dates under a protocol registered before those data were acquired.

That independent test covered 506 paired days across 40 eligible weeks. The revised model achieved approximately −1.0% weekly bias and reduced weekly mean absolute error by about 35% compared with the uncalibrated benchmark on the same data. Our scientific lead approved its publication, limited to dates with complete Terra and Aqua inputs.

We made those decisions visible in the application. The Methodology page shows the results, the earlier failure, and the limitations. Its comparison charts distinguish training dates from previously examined dates and independent-test dates, so agreement during training is not presented as proof of performance.

We also wanted the app to be practical to explore. Users can navigate the calendar with a keyboard, compare years on the same month-and-day axis, and inspect values without relying only on color. The map provides a separate August 2020 detection batch, with optional land-cover and satellite-imagery context.

We used React, TypeScript, Vite, Zod, and Leaflet for the interface, and Python with geospatial libraries for data processing and scientific evaluation. GitHub Actions runs automated checks, and Vercel hosts the application. Codex, Cursor, and Claude/Claude Code assisted with development, testing, documentation, and research diagnostics. The original satellite observations come from the cited data providers; they were not generated by AI.

Our intended users are researchers, environmental analysts, and land managers who need to understand historical fire patterns. We have not yet validated the product with those users, and we see that as an important next step.

The current release also has clear limits. It publishes 635 calibrated estimates, with only six in 2025 and five in 2026. There is no independent backward test. Fire radiative power is an activity indicator, not burned area or a count of individual fires, and ChronoFlare is not a forecasting or emergency-alert system.

What we hope to contribute is a way to make historical comparisons easier to understand and inspect. The Pantanal is our starting point. Expanding to other regions will require further calibration and validation, while keeping the same commitment to showing uncertainty and gaps alongside the results.

Explore the project

Live application: https://chronoflare.vercel.app/

Source code, scientific pipeline and validation evidence: https://github.com/j-c-fstk-dev/chronoflare

dataRefs: NASA Earthdata FIRMS - Detections of active fire hotspots and FRP from MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP), via Standard Processing. Primary source of fire data.
NASA GIBS — MODIS Terra true-color context image, MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor layer. Metrics are not extracted from this image.
projectRefs: IBGE — official boundary of the Pantanal biome, 2025 edition, scale 1:250,000. Spatial reference and subsetting of detections.

MapBiomas Project — land use and land cover, Collection 11, year 2020, 30 m, land cover asset v3. We use this as optional context for the map; it is not used to generate fire hotspots, estimate burned area, or verify sensor coverage.
